newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Canada appeals WTO ruling for U.S. in magazine row.
newsitem.headline: Canada appeals WTO ruling for U.S. in magazine row.

text.p: Canada has told the World Trade Organisation (WTO) it will appeal against a panel ruling that taxes it imposes on Canadian editions of U.S. magazines break global trading rules, trade officials said on Wednesday.

The officials said notification of the appeal in the high-profile dispute was delivered to the WTO on Tuesday, a day before the organisation's Dispute Settlement Body was to consider a U.S. request for adption of the panel report.
Canada has a further 10 days to present the legal basis for its action.
The three-man panel handed down its ruling in February, just under a year after the United States first took the case to the WTO by requesting formal bilateral consultations with Canada.

That followed the imposition in December 1995 by Ottawa of an 80 percent tax on advertising in U.S. periodicals that publish editions in Canada -- an action seen as part of a Canadian effort to protect its domestic publishing industry.
The tax hit the Canadian edition of Sports Illustrated, owned by Time Warner Inc, but Canada's International Trade Minister Art Eggleton argued the affair was a "matter of culture".
Eggleton said that 70 to 90 percent of Canada's cultural industry was dominated by U.S. films and publications.
The law found in violation of the rules by the WTO panel was aimed at "trying to preserve a small piece of our cultural identity," he said in January when the preliminary WTO ruling was issued.

The measure bars income tax deductions for Canadians who advertise in local editions of U.S. magazines. Additionally, postage rates for these publications are higher than rates for nationally-produced periodicals.
Once Canada's formal appeal is delivered to the WTO, an appeals panel will be formed and will have 60 days to hand down its own ruling.
But it can only consider whether the original panel made legal errors in its findings and, under the WTO's dispute settlement procedure, cannot go again into the substance of the dispute.
